This report is in response to that motion.

The administration looked at the mandates of each of the committees and is our normal practice in the past.

So the issue of property tax subclasses for vacant property has a reason before and you will note references in the report to several past reports on this topic.
With respect to the tools available in Saskatchewan, they are limited.
Other jurisdictions in Canada have specific tools in their legislation to create tax policies specific to vacant buildings.
Those tools differ between different jurisdictions and have different purposes or goals depending on the jurisdiction.
A full jurisdiction scan was attached as appendix one to the May 7, 2025 report.
In Saskatchewan, the only tax tool provided to us is the ability to create property tax subclasses.
Different mill rate factors can then be applied to those subclasses to result in a different tax rate for that subclass.
Now, you should be aware that in 2023, the province implemented effective tax rate limits.
And the formula for how that is to be calculated is frankly beyond me, but it is outlined in the regulations of the city's act.
And this section does apply to the inclusion of mill rate factors and may limit how much the city could charge a property using mill rate factors.
There are a couple of municipalities in Saskatchewan that have used property tax subclasses for vacant commercial properties.
In 2014, MooseJaw implemented a property tax subclass for vacant commercial and industrial properties.
In 2017, it was eliminated due to a variety of challenges, including a lack of evidence that had been effective.
The city of North Battleford has created a subclass for vacant commercial property along the key commercial corridor in their city.
The subclass is tied to whether there has been a business license issued for the property in the past two years, and whether there is an active utility account.
The city of Regina is also currently contemplating this issue.
And in November of 2025, their administration presented a report to their executive committee recommending increased enforcement of nuisance properties and no property tax subclass.
The executive committee has deferred consideration of that report twice, and has yet to make a decision on the recommendation of the administration.

In Regina, the administration is not recommending a property tax subclass due to the need for additional resources to implement and maintain the subclass, and says that if this option is chosen, the administration will include a request for resources through the next budget.
The report notes that the administration has achieved outcomes through a proactive engagement approach without the need for a subclass.
In terms of creating a property tax subclass, there are different factors to consider depending on the class of property.
With respect to vacant residential buildings, we have identified a number of potential issues or factors in the report.
Probably the most significant of those issues would be that there is no simple way to identify the properties.
Depending on the goals of the program, different methods could be used to identify the properties, and you certainly see that in other jurisdictions.
But in any case or scenario, the administrative costs to administer such a program would be significant.
With respect to the next class of property outlined in the report being vacant residential land, the program would be much easier to administer.
Partils that are vacant can be identified using the city's assessment records.
However, we would need to consider what property is there like we would like to target, so further analysis could be completed before implementing such a program.
For example, in a newer developing area, it is expected that some lots will remain vacant for a period of time.
Would we want to include those areas? How would we define newer developing?
Would we want to target specific neighborhoods only? Would there be any exemptions or exceptions the city would want to consider?
And then of course, there is the consideration of whether it would be effective.
Would there be a limit on how much the city could charge as an additional tax rate on these properties?
And that would require some additional financial analysis depending on the tax rate of the areas to be targeted.
I have to look at the amount of tax that they currently pay and what adding an additional amount would be due would be enough to discourage keeping the land vacant.
That is difficult to know and would likely require some deeper analysis depending on the areas chosen and other factors.
The last class of property touched on in this report is vacant commercial buildings and land.
Again, depending on whether we target buildings or land, many of the same factors or issues would apply.
This is the class of property that has been the subject of property tax subclasses and other cities with mixed results.
